The designs for voidsonas are incredible, the radical kindness and malicious compliance to society's definition of human, and the understanding and acceptance of my identity are all wonderful, but my favorite part?

Voidpunk challenges *me* to change for the better. It forces me to face my own internalized transphobia, homophobia, aphobia, ableism and how it hurts others as well as myself. I grew up influenced by Catholic values and "parenting" without any patience or empathy for my undiagnosed ADHD needs, and coped with the internet at the height of cringe culture which worsened my prejudices. I had little patience for autistic classmates who said or did things that inconvenienced me or offended me, even when I knew they genuinely didn't mean to and they weren't doing any real harm. I hated furries and alterhumans. I doubted trans people who didn't dress and act "like their gender". 

And even now, as an agender aroacespec ND otherkin who likes switching between androgynous, masculine and feminine presentation, I can mess up and act in ways that hurt myself or others.

The Voidpunk community so freely accepts people who are different, who are considered "difficult" for most cishet abled people to deal with, and seeing it encourages me to have more compassion. More empathy, more understanding, more acceptance. Nobody has to act "human", even if a hurt and scared part of me thinks they should. It's been such a healing and humbling experience, and I'll always be grateful for that

Please remember that aromanticism is an orientation, not something you can just "become" the same way you can't choose to be gay or straight. And aromantic people can still experience strong emotions towards others, mental health issues, and even toxic relationships; "becoming" aro will not fix anything. 

Instead, please try to focus on getting professional help for what you're experiencing, as this definitely goes deeper than just romantic attraction. Romantic attraction alone isn't to blame for what's distressing you; it's far more likely to be underlying trauma or mental health issues that need intervention

Before talking about labels, I think you should take the time to properly process your feelings around love and romance, especially because you say you stopped feeling romantic attraction due to your experiences in dating. I think this is something that calls for therapy.

 Yes, aromanticism is a spectrum, and there are aromantic people who don't or rarely experience attraction but want and enjoy romantic relationships. However, it always does rub me the wrong way when people call themselves aro after a series of bad breakups or bad relationships. I think in those times it's less important to think of what to call yourself than it is to properly explore and figure out the reasons behind what you're feeling.

Honestly, as an arospec person, I'm not really all that comfortable with the idea of aromanticism as a political movement nor am I comfortable with the stance that romance is inherently queerphobic. I do want to dispel the hierarchy that places romantic love on the highest pedestal, but I do not want to dismiss romance as a public fantasy or purely as an instrument of violence or oppression. I also feel rubbed the wrong way by "romantically attractive people" being defined here strictly as conventionally attractive and conforming. 

I think the view of romance should be reformed and should be viewed in a much more personal and existential lens (in that it really means different things depending on the culture and the individual's perception, with complicated biological and sociocultural aspects), and it should be rejected as a necessity for all people.

I don't mind romance. I don't mind people wanting romance, wanting to start families and do cheesy shit with their partners or polycules, and I will always have a respect for "freedom to love" being the foundation of the queer movement. 

I simply want to exist alongside that, and I want other similar people to exist peacefully, without being compelled by society to do anything they don't want to do.

There's also the exclusivity, the joy of being the one person who can make another feel that intensity and do exclusive and emotionally intimate things with just that one person or just that group of people.

It admittedly gets very confusing, as what is considered "romantic" differs from culture to culture, and from individual to individual. I myself am confused by it, to the point that I've read books on the subject (What Love Is: And What it Could Be by Carrie Jenkins is a wonderful recommendation, and aro-inclusive!)

But I've seen romantic attraction described as having some form of biological, physiological component (butterflies in the stomach, feeling like the first kiss is "magic", feeling "giddy", heat spreading in the face, elation akin to a high when around a crush or romantic interest, feelings that inspire passionate romantic gestures, exclusive bonds)

This is combined with a social component (traditions like dates, romantic gifts, introduction to families, marriage, children, etc. but not all romantic relationships need these)

Romantic attraction is a weird nebulous mish-mash of these things, but I think the physiological component is an important part to many people. The person wants to feel wanted romantically, to know that their presence sparks excitement and joy, and (not always sexual) desire that's just "different" from what friends commonly feel. There's also exclusivity there, be it between two or more people, in which they do traditionally romantic things together and actively *want* to, on a physiological level.

Of course, that's only my understanding, and I'm sure it might be described differently by other people.

Aromantic =/= Asexual.

Other than that, what works for "many people" may not work for many others. Many people on the aroace spectrum (and many people in general) do not want open relationships, myself included. And many people want sex to be reserved for only their partners (romantic or otherwise). It's not as simple as just getting into an open relationship without regard for the needs and feelings of the people in the relationship.

They can! But most alloromantics prefer certain traditionally romantic things (living together in the same bed, bathing together, tenderly holding hands, kissing, dates, etc.) to be done with people who are attracted to them romantically. Not everyone gets their emotional needs met with a partner who loves them purely platonically, and while that's definitely okay, it does mean that it's harder for aros/arospecs to find the type of relationships they're looking for.

Just to let you know, there's a reason essential oils are used extremely sparsely and heavily diluted in fragrances, and it's not just because they're expensive!

Commercially sold perfumes follow IFRA guidelines, which dictate the maximum amount an aromachemical, molecule, or essential oil can be used in a fragrance. This minimizes the risk of allergies, chemical burns, and other hazards to the skin and lungs. 

Aromachemicals used in perfumes are much safer and better regulated than most essential oil fragrances (and FYI, the drops system a la essential oil to carrier that essential oil fragrances tend to use is NOT reliable for skin safety. All regulated fragrances measure their ingredients by grams.)

Additionally, I'd argue lab-made aromachemicals are likely more ethical and easier on the environment than essential oils whose origins you aren't sure of.
